question: To whom is the epistle of Philippians addressed in the opening salutation of Philippians 1:1?
opt1: To all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons
opt2: To the chief magistrate and proconsul presiding over the colony of Macedonia
opt3: To the high priest and rulers of the synagogue residing in Neapolis
opt4: To the Roman centurions stationed at the garrison of Philippi
correct: To all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons
explanation: Paul and Timothy address the entire assembly in Philippi, specifically identifying both overseers (bishops) and deacons. Philippians 1:1 (KJV) - "Paul and Timotheus, the servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons:"

question: What confident assurance does Paul express concerning the ongoing work of God in believers in Philippians 1:6?
opt1: Believers must complete their redemption through their own moral perfection
opt2: He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ
opt3: God abandons His purpose whenever believers face physical affliction
opt4: The work of salvation remains incomplete until certified by Jerusalem elders
correct: He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ
explanation: Paul is fully confident that God's sovereign grace initiates, sustains, and will bring to ultimate completion His redemptive work in believers. Philippians 1:6 (KJV) - "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:"

question: What does Paul pray will abound more and more in the Philippian believers in Philippians 1:9?
opt1: That your personal financial fortunes might increase throughout Macedonia
opt2: That your municipal political influence might dominate Roman magistrates
opt3: That your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and in all judgment
opt4: That your physical strength might never diminish through aging
correct: That your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and in all judgment
explanation: Paul prays that their Christian love will not be blind sentimentality, but rich in spiritual discernment and full knowledge. Philippians 1:9 (KJV) - "And this I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and in all judgment;"

question: How had Paul's imprisonment in Rome unexpectedly affected the spread of the gospel in Philippians 1:12-13?
opt1: His imprisonment completely silenced the preaching of the cross in Italy
opt2: His bonds caused all Gentile disciples to abandon the Christian faith
opt3: His captivity compelled the Roman senate to outlaw all foreign religions
opt4: The things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel; so that my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace
correct: The things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel; so that my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace
explanation: Paul's imprisonment actually advanced the gospel, making his witness for Christ widely known throughout the imperial praetorium. Philippians 1:12-13 (KJV) - "But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel; So that my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace, and in all other places;"

question: What mixed motives did Paul observe among those who preached Christ in Rome during his imprisonment in Philippians 1:15-18?
opt1: Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will... whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice
opt2: All preachers were certified by written decrees from the twelve apostles in Jerusalem
opt3: Every minister sought exclusively personal financial gain through mandatory collections
opt4: Preachers were prohibited from speaking unless they had witnessed the earthly ministry of Jesus
correct: Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will... whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice
explanation: Even when rivals preached out of partisan jealousy to afflict Paul in his bonds, he rejoiced because Christ was being proclaimed. Philippians 1:15-18 (KJV) - "Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will: The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds: But the other of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel. What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice."

question: What earnest expectation and hope did Paul cherish regarding his physical body in Philippians 1:20?
opt1: That he might secure an imperial pardon and retire to his hometown of Tarsus
opt2: That with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death
opt3: That he might avoid all bodily suffering and execution at the hands of Roman guards
opt4: That he might be acclaimed as a great philosopher in the academies of Athens
correct: That with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death
explanation: Paul's single supreme ambition was that Jesus Christ would be glorified and magnified in his mortal body, whether by continued life or martyrdom. Philippians 1:20 (KJV) - "According to my earnest expectation and my hope, that in nothing I shall be ashamed, but that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death."

question: What famous motto of personal life and death did the apostle articulate in Philippians 1:21?
opt1: To live is knowledge, and to die is oblivion
opt2: To live is honor, and to die is tragedy
opt3: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain
opt4: To live is virtue, and to die is fate
correct: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain
explanation: For Paul, Christ was the very essence, source, and purpose of earthly existence; hence dying meant gaining unhindered union with Him. Philippians 1:21 (KJV) - "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain."

question: Between what two desires was Paul pulled in a strait in Philippians 1:23-24?
opt1: Desiring to travel to Spain versus retiring permanently in Antioch
opt2: Seeking civil political office in Rome versus returning to Jerusalem
opt3: Wishing to accumulate books in Ephesus versus preaching in Athens
opt4: Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better: nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you
correct: Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better: nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you
explanation: Paul longed for personal departure to be with Christ, yet recognized that remaining in the flesh was necessary for their spiritual progress. Philippians 1:23-24 (KJV) - "For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better: Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you."

question: How does Paul exhort the Philippian congregation to conduct themselves as citizens of the gospel in Philippians 1:27?
opt1: Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ... that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel
opt2: Petition the Roman provincial governor for special municipal tax exemptions
opt3: Observe all Jewish ceremonial fasts and feasts with utmost exactness
opt4: Withdraw completely from secular civil duties to reside in the mountains
correct: Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ... that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel
explanation: Believers are urged to live worthy of their heavenly citizenship, standing united in one spirit and contending together for gospel truth. Philippians 1:27 (KJV) - "Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;"

question: What twofold privilege is granted unto believers in the behalf of Christ in Philippians 1:29?
opt1: To escape all earthly tribulation and enjoy perpetual financial prosperity
opt2: Not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake
opt3: To govern the civil assemblies and dictate secular laws across Macedonia
opt4: To receive private revelations forbidden to the rest of the congregation
correct: Not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake
explanation: Suffering for Christ is not a divine accident or curse, but a sacred grace granted alongside saving faith. Philippians 1:29 (KJV) - "For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake;"

question: What attitude of humility toward others does Paul command the believers to maintain in Philippians 2:3?
opt1: Assert your personal authority and demand unquestioned submission from all members
opt2: Compete for the highest ecclesiastical titles and public recognition in the city
opt3: Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves
opt4: Isolate yourself from fellowship whenever others fail to recognize your gifts
correct: Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves
explanation: Christian unity requires the repudiation of selfish rivalry and conceit, cultivating humble deference that values others above oneself. Philippians 2:3 (KJV) - "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves."

question: Whose supreme example of humility and self-emptying are believers exhorted to adopt in Philippians 2:5-7?
opt1: The philosophical stoicism exemplified by the Greek sages of Athens
opt2: The military discipline demonstrated by Roman centurions of the praetorium
opt3: The ascetic fasting practiced by the desert hermits near the Salt Sea
opt4: Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God... made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant
correct: Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God... made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant
explanation: Christ possessed full essential deity, yet emptied Himself (Kenosis) by taking the form of a servant in true human likeness. Philippians 2:5-7 (KJV) - "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:"

question: To what ultimate depth of obedient humiliation did Jesus Christ descend in Philippians 2:8?
opt1: He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross
opt2: He surrendered His divine nature permanently and ceased to be God
opt3: He served as a secular magistrate executing the decrees of Caesar
opt4: He withdrew to the wilderness to avoid all contact with mortal men
correct: He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross
explanation: Christ's voluntary obedience reached its absolute climax in submitting to the most shameful, agonizing death: the death of the cross. Philippians 2:8 (KJV) - "And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross."

question: How has God the Father responded to Christ's self-humiliation according to Philippians 2:9-11?
opt1: God granted Him an earthly palace on Mount Zion with thousands of physical soldiers
opt2: Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow
opt3: God made Him an honorary counselor to the high court of the Sanhedrin
opt4: God restricted His authority exclusively to the land of Palestine and Syria
correct: Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow
explanation: Because of Christ's supreme obedience, God exalted Him to universal sovereignty, demanding universal confession that He is Lord. Philippians 2:9-11 (KJV) - "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father."

question: What balance between human responsibility and divine sovereignty is taught in Philippians 2:12-13?
opt1: Earn your eternal redemption through ritual washings, for God remains entirely passive
opt2: Relax in passive slumber, for God requires no human obedience or moral effort
opt3: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure
opt4: Rely exclusively on ancestral lineage, for salvation is determined by genealogical birth
correct: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure
explanation: Believers are to work out the practical fruits of their salvation reverently, empowered by God who energizes both the desire and the deed. Philippians 2:12-13 (KJV) - "Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure."

question: How are believers to conduct their daily activities in a crooked world in Philippians 2:14-15?
opt1: Engage in public protests and civil disobedience against municipal taxes
opt2: Debate aggressively in the market square to prove intellectual superiority
opt3: Conform quietly to popular pagan festivities to avoid social friction
opt4: Do all things without murmurings and disputings: that ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God... among whom ye shine as lights in the world
correct: Do all things without murmurings and disputings: that ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God... among whom ye shine as lights in the world
explanation: A grumbling, contentious spirit darkens Christian testimony; harmonious, blameless living shines like radiant stars in a dark generation. Philippians 2:14-15 (KJV) - "Do all things without murmurings and disputings: That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world;"

question: What sacrificial metaphor does Paul apply to his own life and ministry in Philippians 2:17?
opt1: Yea, and if I be offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I joy, and rejoice with you all
opt2: I am as an undefeated general marching through the triumphal arches of Rome
opt3: I serve as a high priest demanding golden vessels for the sanctuary of Ephesus
opt4: I stand as an imperial ambassador immune from all physical mortality
correct: Yea, and if I be offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I joy, and rejoice with you all
explanation: Paul viewed his potential martyrdom as a joyful drink offering (libation) poured out upon the sacrificial service of their faith. Philippians 2:17 (KJV) - "Yea, and if I be offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I joy, and rejoice with you all."

question: Why did Paul desire to send Timothy to Philippi, highly commending his character in Philippians 2:19-20?
opt1: Because Timothy possessed large personal wealth to build a meetinghouse in Philippi
opt2: For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state. For all seek their own, not the things which are Jesus Christ's
opt3: Because Timothy was a native citizen of Philippi holding high political office
opt4: Because Timothy was trained in the legal codes of the Roman imperial senate
correct: For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state. For all seek their own, not the things which are Jesus Christ's
explanation: Timothy stood out as uniquely selfless and genuine, possessing an authentic pastoral heart that sought Christ's interests rather than his own. Philippians 2:20-21 (KJV) - "For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state. For all seek their own, not the things which are Jesus Christ's."

question: Who was the messenger sent by the Philippians to minister to Paul's needs who became sick nigh unto death in Philippians 2:25-27?
opt1: Tychicus the faithful minister from the province of Asia
opt2: Erastus the chamberlain of the city of Corinth
opt3: Epaphroditus, my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants
opt4: Onesiphorus who often refreshed Paul in Rome
correct: Epaphroditus, my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants
explanation: Epaphroditus brought the Philippians' financial gift to Paul in Rome, risking his life and falling critically ill in gospel service. Philippians 2:25 (KJV) - "Yet I supposed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants."

question: Why were the Philippians instructed to hold Epaphroditus in high spiritual reputation in Philippians 2:29-30?
opt1: Because he secured imperial letters of protection from Caesar
opt2: Because he performed public miracles before the magistrates of Philippi
opt3: Because he negotiated a commercial trade contract for Macedonian churches
opt4: Because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me
correct: Because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me
explanation: Epaphroditus was worthy of double honor because he hazardous his very life (paraboleusamenos) to complete their ministry of love to Paul. Philippians 2:30 (KJV) - "Because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me."

question: Against what group of legalistic false teachers does Paul issue a sharp threefold warning in Philippians 3:2?
opt1: Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision
opt2: Beware of the Stoic philosophers, the Epicureans, and the Roman tax collectors
opt3: Beware of the silversmiths, the carpenters, and the merchant sea captains
opt4: Beware of the municipal clerks, the prison wardens, and the centurions
correct: Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision
explanation: Paul uses harsh terms to denounce the Judaizers: calling them spiritual scavengers (dogs), evil workers, and mutilators of the flesh (concision). Philippians 3:2 (KJV) - "Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision."

question: Who does Paul declare are the true circumcision in Philippians 3:3?
opt1: Those who bear the physical mark of Abraham performed on the eighth day
opt2: Which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh
opt3: Those who observe all ceremonial new moons and Sabbath fastings in Jerusalem
opt4: Those who can trace biological descent from the twelve sons of Jacob
correct: Which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh
explanation: True spiritual circumcision is inward, characterized by Spirit-led worship, boasting exclusively in Christ, and zero reliance on fleshly pedigree. Philippians 3:3 (KJV) - "For we are the circumcision, which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh."

question: What impressive Jewish credentials and legal pedigree did Paul list in Philippians 3:5-6?
opt1: Born of the priestly tribe of Levi, an high priest consecrated by the Sanhedrin
opt2: A royal prince of the house of David, a governor appointed over Judea
opt3: Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee
opt4: A scribe of the school of Alexandria, a master of Greek and Persian wisdom
correct: Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee
explanation: Paul possessed an impeccably pure pedigree: covenant circumcision, Israelite ancestry, Benjamin tribe, strict Pharisaic observance, and blameless zeal. Philippians 3:5 (KJV) - "Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee;"

question: How did Paul evaluate his prestigious religious pedigree after encountering Christ in Philippians 3:7-8?
opt1: He considered them valuable assets to be blended harmoniously with the gospel
opt2: He preserved them as secret qualifications to be unveiled before Roman courts
opt3: He viewed them as absolute proof that he deserved divine salvation
opt4: What things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ... and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ
correct: What things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ... and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ
explanation: All former religious achievements were reclassified as worthless garbage (skubala / dung) in comparison to the supreme treasure of knowing Christ. Philippians 3:7-8 (KJV) - "But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,"

question: What righteousness did Paul seek to be found in, according to Philippians 3:9?
opt1: Not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith
opt2: A righteousness earned by strict compliance to the oral traditions of the elders
opt3: A civic virtue recognized and commended by the Roman proconsul
opt4: A philosophical moral perfection achieved through personal ascetic discipline
correct: Not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith
explanation: Paul discarded self-righteousness derived from the law, relying solely on imputed divine righteousness received through faith in Christ. Philippians 3:9 (KJV) - "And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:"

question: What three supreme desires of intimate fellowship with Christ did Paul articulate in Philippians 3:10?
opt1: That I may establish large meetinghouses, write books, and gain fame among Greeks
opt2: That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death
opt3: That I may escape all bodily illness, receive gold from merchants, and rule in Philippi
opt4: That I may overthrow the Roman emperor and establish a theocratic kingdom on earth
correct: That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death
explanation: Paul yearned for experiential knowledge of Christ: experiencing His resurrection power, sharing His sufferings, and being conformed to His cross. Philippians 3:10 (KJV) - "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death;"

question: What athletic metaphor does Paul employ to describe his single-minded spiritual pursuit in Philippians 3:13-14?
opt1: Wrestling against wild beasts in the municipal arena of Ephesus for public acclaim
opt2: Navigating a merchant galley through storm-tossed seas to reach the port of Rome
opt3: Forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus
opt4: Boxing with shadows in the gymnastic school to display athletic prowess
correct: Forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus
explanation: Like an Olympic runner with eyes fixed ahead, Paul forgot past achievements and strained every nerve toward the eternal prize. Philippians 3:13-14 (KJV) - "Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus."

question: How does Paul describe the tragic character and destiny of the enemies of the cross of Christ in Philippians 3:18-19?
opt1: Whose minds are enlightened by profound philosophy and who inherit eternal glory
opt2: Who shall be pardoned without repentance on the day of final judgment
opt3: Who are merely misguided seekers worthy of ecclesiastical leadership
opt4: Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things
correct: Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things
explanation: Sensual antinomians make their appetites their god, glorying in shameful conduct and facing eternal ruin. Philippians 3:19 (KJV) - "Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)"

question: Where is the true citizenship (conversation) of the believer located in Philippians 3:20?
opt1: For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ
opt2: In the imperial capital of Rome under the protection of Caesar's law
opt3: In the holy city of Jerusalem within the courts of the earthly temple
opt4: In the municipal archives of the colony of Philippi in Macedonia
correct: For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ
explanation: While living on earth, believers hold their true citizenship (politeuma) in heaven, eagerly anticipating the return of their Savior. Philippians 3:20 (KJV) - "For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:"

question: What glorious bodily transformation will the Lord Jesus Christ accomplish at His return in Philippians 3:21?
opt1: He will dissolve our bodies into ethereal spirits with no physical form
opt2: Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body
opt3: He will preserve our mortal bodies in their present fallen condition forever
opt4: He will return our souls to the primitive state of earthly dust
correct: Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body
explanation: By His sovereign omnipotence, Christ will transform our frail, mortal bodies to match His own glorified, indestructible resurrection body. Philippians 3:21 (KJV) - "Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself."

question: Which two Christian women does Paul entreat to reconcile and be of the same mind in the Lord in Philippians 4:2?
opt1: Priscilla and Phoebe of Cenchrea
opt2: Mary and Martha of Bethany
opt3: I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord
opt4: Lydia and Damaris of Athens
correct: I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord
explanation: Paul directly appeals to Euodias and Syntyche, two prominent co-workers in the gospel, to resolve their interpersonal disagreement in the Lord. Philippians 4:2 (KJV) - "I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord."

question: What joyful command does Paul repeat emphatically in Philippians 4:4?
opt1: Fast forty days before the feast of Passover: and again I say, Fast
opt2: Demand your legal rights before the magistrate: and again I say, Demand
opt3: Retreat into solitude from the world: and again I say, Retreat
opt4: Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice
correct: Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice
explanation: Christian joy is independent of external circumstances; it is rooted immovably in the Lord Himself, commanding continual praise. Philippians 4:4 (KJV) - "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice."

question: What divine remedy does Paul prescribe for anxiety and worry in Philippians 4:6?
opt1: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God
opt2: Consult the astrological charts to prepare for future calamities
opt3: Borrow money from wealthy patrons to eliminate financial uncertainty
opt4: Suppress all conscious emotion through rigid Stoic detachment
correct: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God
explanation: Worry is banished by turning every concern into prayer and thankful petition before God. Philippians 4:6 (KJV) - "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God."

question: What will the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, do for the praying believer in Philippians 4:7?
opt1: Grant immediate exemption from all earthly taxation and civic duties
opt2: Shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus
opt3: Eliminate all biological need for sleep and physical sustenance
opt4: Promote the believer to political governance in the province
correct: Shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus
explanation: God's transcendent peace acts like a vigilant garrison (phroureo), guarding the believer's inner heart and thoughts in Christ Jesus. Philippians 4:7 (KJV) - "And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus."

question: Upon what six noble qualities are believers instructed to fix their thoughts in Philippians 4:8?
opt1: Whatsoever things bring wealth, whatsoever things bring fame, whatsoever things bring power, whatsoever things bring ease
opt2: Whatsoever things criticize others, whatsoever things foster suspicion, whatsoever things provoke debate
opt3: Whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report
opt4: Whatsoever things relate to the genealogies of the patriarchs and the traditions of the scribes
correct: Whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report
explanation: Paul commands believers to deliberately direct their thought life toward whatever is morally excellent, authentic, lovely, and praiseworthy. Philippians 4:8 (KJV) - "Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things."

question: What great secret of contentment did Paul learn through the varied experiences of his ministry in Philippians 4:11-12?
opt1: He learned to demand fixed salaries from every church he established
opt2: He learned to abandon gospel preaching whenever resources became scarce
opt3: He learned to borrow silver from Roman merchants during lean seasons
opt4: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound
correct: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound
explanation: Contentment was a learned spiritual grace; Paul remained inwardly satisfied and serene whether experiencing abundance or deprivation. Philippians 4:11-12 (KJV) - "Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need."

question: What triumphant declaration of spiritual ability and divine enablement does Paul make in Philippians 4:13?
